name: money
title: Future me
tagline: Money moves for your twenties in Canada
notice: General education, not personal financial advice. Limits change every year, so check the CRA site for the current numbers.

start.title: Start with small amounts
steps: Pick an amount you will not miss: $25 a paycheque is enough to start.
Set an automatic transfer for the day after payday.
Put it in a TFSA so growth is never taxed.
Raise the amount by a little every time your pay goes up.
start.urgent: The habit matters more than the amount. Starting at 22 instead of 32 roughly doubles what the same deposits become by 65.

tfsa_rrsp.title: TFSA or RRSP
steps: TFSA: you pay tax now, and growth and withdrawals are tax-free. Withdrawn room comes back the next calendar year.
RRSP: you get a tax deduction now and pay tax when you withdraw in retirement.
Lower income today: fill the TFSA first.
Higher income today than you expect in retirement: the RRSP deduction is worth more.
Unused room in both carries forward, so nothing is lost by waiting on the RRSP.
tfsa_rrsp.urgent: Over-contributing to either costs 1% a month on the excess. Check your room on CRA My Account first.

fhsa.title: First home savings account
steps: Open an FHSA if you are 18 or older and have not owned a home recently.
You can put in up to $8,000 a year, to a lifetime total of $40,000.
Contributions reduce your taxable income, like an RRSP.
Withdrawals to buy a first home are tax-free, like a TFSA.
If you never buy, the money can move to your RRSP without using RRSP room.
fhsa.urgent: Room only starts building once the account is open, so open it early even with a small deposit.

match.title: Employer matching
steps: Ask HR whether there is a group RRSP or pension with matching.
Contribute at least enough to get the full match.
A 50% or 100% match is an instant return no investment can promise.
Check the vesting rule: how long you must stay to keep the employer's money.
match.urgent: Skipping the match is turning down part of your pay.

emergency.title: Emergency fund
steps: Start with a first goal of $1,000.
Build toward three months of rent, food and bills.
Keep it in a high-interest savings account, not invested.
Use it only for real emergencies, then refill it.
emergency.urgent: Without a cushion, one surprise bill goes on a credit card at about 20% interest.

compound.title: Why starting early wins
steps: Growth earns its own growth, so time does most of the work.
$200 a month from age 22 to 65 at 6% grows to about $485,000.
The same $200 a month from age 32 grows to about $250,000.
Ten years of delay costs almost half the result.
compound.urgent: These figures are before inflation and assume a steady 6%, which real markets do not deliver every year.

debt.title: Pay debt or invest
steps: List each debt with its interest rate.
Credit cards at about 20%: pay these off before investing anything.
Student loans at a low rate: pay the minimum and invest alongside.
Always take an employer match first, even with debt.
debt.urgent: No investment reliably beats 20% card interest. Clearing it is the best return available.

budget.title: A budget that survives
steps: Take your monthly pay after tax.
About 50% for needs: rent, food, transit, phone.
About 30% for wants.
About 20% for savings and extra debt payments, moved automatically on payday.
If rent pushes needs over 50%, cut wants first and keep at least 10% for savings.
budget.urgent: Track one month of real spending before you set the numbers.

index.title: What to invest in
steps: A broad index fund or all-in-one ETF holds thousands of companies in one purchase.
Look for a management fee (MER) under about 0.25%.
A 2% fee can eat roughly a third of your result over 40 years.
Buy on a schedule and do not check it daily.
index.urgent: Picking single stocks or crypto with money you need is speculation, not a retirement plan.

credit.title: Build your credit score
steps: Get one no-fee credit card and use it for a regular small bill.
Pay the full statement balance every month, on time.
Keep the balance under 30% of the limit.
Keep your oldest card open.
credit.urgent: One missed payment stays on your report for about six years.
